claims.text: Droid implements programmatic tool calling (PTC) as a Script tool: the model writes JavaScript that runs in a sandbox with no file, network, or system access of its own.
In Droid's Script tool, raw files, search results, and logs stay inside the program, only printed output returns to the model, and independent calls run concurrently.
A single Droid Script can make hundreds of tool calls in one model request, so instructions and history are sent once rather than re-sent every few calls.
In a Droid Linear cleanup task, 151 issues were moved and verified in 312 tool calls using 2 requests and about 61,000 tokens, versus about 36 requests and 3.1M tokens when models direct calls.
A Droid CI sweep covered 5,384 jobs across 547 runs in 2 requests.
On Claude Opus 5.5, Script mode cuts Droid's cost by 15% versus direct tool calling.
In a unit test fix example, time in model calls fell from 42.3 s to 28.0 s and the task finished in 41.6 s instead of 56.8 s.

Droid originally ran multiple sessions as separate processes of about 350 MB each (over 2 GB for five parallel subagents plus the main session); sessions now share the daemon's process at about 20 MB each, and /new is instant.

Droid runs interactively in a terminal UI with approvals and MCP tools, or non-interactively via droid exec, which carries a single task to completion and returns text, JSON, or stream-jsonrpc output.
Droid reads AGENTS.md files for project guidance on architecture, build/test commands, and conventions before making changes.
Droid sessions can be resumed with droid --resume or duplicated with /fork, and a Sessions API gives programmatic access to running and completed sessions.

Given a task, a Droid first inspects the environment (codebase, Git branch, machine capabilities), recovers relevant history including user and organization memories, proposes a plan and asks clarifying questions, then writes code, runs pre-commit hooks and linting, and generates a pull request.
Custom Droids are subagents defined as Markdown files with their own system prompt, model, and tool set, invoked via the Task tool at a chosen complexity level in the foreground or background.

A custom droid runs in a fresh context, can use a different model, can be restricted to read-only, edit, execute, web, or selected MCP servers, returns one result, and cannot ask the user or recursively create another subagent.
Reyes sketches eight tickets assigned across eight code Droids, with dependencies determining which work can run in parallel.
Missions enable long-horizon, multi-step, multi-agent workflows in which specialist Droids coordinate across SDLC stages.
Droid's Autonomy Level (Off, Low, Medium, High) determines which commands and MCP tools run without asking, and a built-in blocklist prevents certain destructive commands at any level.
Droid's sandbox checks for read, write, and network access run independently of the Autonomy Level and can force additional approvals; in headless mode droid exec fails fast on permission violations.
Factory's optional OS-level sandbox (Beta) provides kernel-enforced filesystem and network isolation, and Droid Computers provide Factory-managed cloud sandboxes on Plus/Max plans.

Every new model is added to Droid by automation, checked against behavioral assertions, then evaluated via live environments, QA, and daily benchmark runs, with live error logs and user friction added to benchmark failures for review.
Most Droid changes came from an internal Agent Factory loop in which agents read failures and propose changes, tested on every affected model family, with engineers reviewing and merging.

On Terminal-Bench 4 (self-reported), Droid scored 65.2% with Claude Opus 5.5 versus Cursor and OpenCode 62.1%, Devin 59.6%, and Claude Code 57.6%, at up to 24% lower cost; the best result cost $4.73 per passed task.
With GPT-6.1 Sol on Terminal-Bench 4, Droid scored 57.6% at $0.79 per passed task versus Codex 54.0%, OpenCode 51.0%, and Devin 45.0%.
On Opus 5.5, Droid takes 26% less time per passed task and uses 17% fewer tokens than Claude Code; on GPT-6.1 Sol it uses 12% fewer tokens than Codex but takes 10% longer.

Factory's Terminal-Bench 4 comparison used three trials per task from October 23 to 28, 2026, counting cost and time only on tasks both harnesses passed in all three trials; the results are vendor-published, not independent.
